text: DLC directly schedules vehicle charging to achieve a desired aggregate response. For example, DLC can coordinate EV charging with availability of bulk power system supply-side resources, or to flatten peak electricity load. Because this process minimally involves two-way communication between vehicles or chargers and grid operators, DLC is often facilitated by a third party responsible for presenting a megawatt-scale aggregate of individual vehicle charging flexibility to the power system operator. The third-party “aggregator” then takes responsibility for fulfilling the resulting dispatch requests by scheduling individual vehicle charging. In contrast, price-responsive dispatch mechanisms can use one-way communication of time-varying prices to individual vehicles, chargers, or drivers. Price-responsive mechanisms rely on individual behavioral or automated responses to communicated prices to coordinate charging demand. For example, electricity tariff designs like time-of-use (TOU) rates and hourly real-time prices (RTP) offered to electric utility customers are price-responsive dispatch mechanisms that incentivize EV charging during lower-price hours. The primary contribution of this report is to show how price-responsive mechanisms with one- way communication and lower implementation costs than DLC can overcome documented issues with electricity demand spikes resulting from simultaneous price-response. Overcoming these issues makes price-responsive mechanisms preferable to DLC at higher shares of LDVs participating in EVMC. Two strategies are particularly effective in integrating double-digit percentage shares of LDVs in price-responsive EVMC: (1) simultaneous responses to price minima/maxima are forecast and anticipated in bulk power system dispatch and (2) individual vehicle charging is flattened over the same-priced hours when EVs are plugged in. These findings differ from recent work (The AES Corporation and Camus 2024; EnergyHub, Inc. 2024) suggesting more DLC-like active management will be necessary in the coming decade for managing EV charging to avoid costly simultaneous response to prices. This report softens that prescription by further exploring an earlier finding that DLC and price-responsive mechanisms both have advantages and disadvantages (Hale et al. 2022a). Scenarios developed in this work directly compare our formulation of DLC to price-responsive mechanisms in a realistic bulk power system model. There are coordination mechanisms in the literature that blend DLC and price-responsive approaches by sending individualized price 1 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. signals (like price-responsive mechanisms) to achieve a coordinated outcome (like DLC). However, such methods are mostly iterative and can thus be considered a variant of, or a specific way to implement, DLC (Xi and Sioshansi 2014; Cutler et al. 2021; Najafi and Fripp 2023). Noniterative mechanisms that send individualized price signals to consumers or devices can produce a coordinated shed response (Cole, Morton, and Edgar 2014), but we are unaware of any such mechanisms able to coordinate energy shifting. Thus, we subsume mechanisms that send individualized price signals to achieve a coordinated outcome under the broader category of DLC in this study and proceed comparing price-responsive and DLC mechanisms. The primary advantage of DLC is that, because it directly coordinates EV charging load with electricity supply, it is guaranteed to lower overall electricity costs no matter how many vehicles participate.
